# Brake Bleed Sequence for Chevrolet Suburban 2015

When working on a 2015 Chevrolet Suburban LTZ 4WD equipped with StabiliTrak, the expectation that "farthest from closest" to the master cylinder is a universal rule often breaks down in practice. While this sequence works well for standard hydraulic systems, the combination of an electronic stability control module and a rear differential with internal bleeder valves introduces specific constraints that can leave you staring at air bubbles refusing to exit the rear calipers or wheel cylinders.

The scenario you describedâfront brakes bleeding quickly while the rear remain stubbornâis a classic symptom of either trapped air in the flexible hose assembly within the axle or an incomplete purge of the StabiliTrak system before attempting to bleed the wheels. Replacing lines with steel braided hoses is a sound upgrade for durability, but these lines often require a specific priming step that standard rubber lines do not. If the new lines were not fully filled with fluid before connecting them to the bleeder valves or calipers, you will inevitably trap air pockets that resist expulsion under normal gravity bleed pressure.

### The StabiliTrak Dependency

Before touching a wrench on the rear wheels, the electronic stability control system must be acknowledged. Modern GM platforms of this era integrate the brake master cylinder and wheel sensors into a closed loop managed by the ABS/StabiliTrak module. If you have opened the bleeder valves without first ensuring the fluid reservoir is topped off to the absolute brim, or if you have not re-primed the system after installing new lines, you risk introducing air directly into the pump mechanism.

The correct procedure involves a two-stage approach. First, you must perform a system flush or at least a thorough top-off and purge of the master cylinder while the vehicle is off. This ensures the internal reservoir and any associated valves are free of voids. Once confirmed, you can proceed to the wheels. However, simply following the diagonal pattern may not suffice if the rear axle hoses were replaced. The flexible rubber hose running from the axle to the caliper or wheel cylinder often contains a small air pocket near the bleeder valve itself if it was disconnected and reconnected. This specific location acts as a sump where air settles regardless of the order in which you open the other three wheels.

### Addressing the Rear Axle Hoses

If you have replaced the brake lines including those running to the rear axle, the issue is likely located within the flexible hose on the differential side rather than the rigid steel line. When disconnecting a bleeder valve or caliper to install new hardware, air enters the flexible hose. Because the bleeder valve on the wheel cylinder or caliper is often positioned at a slight angle relative to gravity, air can get trapped in the bend of the rubber hose if it wasn't purged prior to tightening the connection.

To resolve this without disassembling the axle again, you must use the pressure bleed method or a vacuum extractor while actively manipulating the flexible hose. While the wheel is mounted and the bleeder valve is open, gently flexing the rubber hose at the connection point near the caliper or wheel cylinder can help dislodge trapped air bubbles that are floating against the flow of fluid. This mechanical agitation forces the air out of the low spot in the hose and into the main stream where it can be expelled through the bleeder valve.

### Implementation Strategy

If gravity bleeding fails to clear the rear lines, switch to a pressure bleed setup using a nitrogen tank or a dedicated pressure tool set to 10â15 PSI. Connect the kit to the master cylinder and open all four bleeder valves sequentially. The pressure forces fluid through the entire system, including the stubborn flexible hoses in the rear axle, much faster than gravity alone can achieve.

Monitor the master cylinder reservoir constantly. If it drops too low during this high-volume flush, you will suck air back into the pump, undoing your progress. Keep the fluid level above the max line at all times. Once the pressure bleed is complete and no bubbles appear in the output of any valve over two consecutive cycles, close the valves and let the system settle.

If the brakes still feel spongy after confirming the lines are full and the reservoir is topped off, the master cylinder internal seals may be compromised by air that entered during the line replacement. In rare cases, a stuck ABS modulator valve can also prevent proper fluid circulation to the rear wheels. However, given your description of fast front bleeding, the culprit is almost certainly trapped air in the rear flexible hoses or an incomplete initial purge of the StabiliTrak module. Ensure you have followed the specific reset procedure for the StabiliTrak system if the vehicle detects a fault code after the service.
